title: Stakeholders and key influencers in the scenario
blurb: Pick the key influencer from a people list, spot every stakeholder, read the culture and choose the OCM action that fits.
question: At Draycott Precision Engineering, experienced maintenance engineers doubt that a dashboard can predict machine failures. Which person in the people list is MOST LIKELY to be a key influencer for the engineers' adoption of the change?

teach.h: Stakeholders: wider than the project team
teach.body: In organizational change management, a stakeholder is any individual, group or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by the change initiative. Plain English: if people think the change touches them, they are stakeholders, whether or not they are right and whether or not they hold a project role. A union, a tenants' panel or a carers' network can be a stakeholder with no seat on the board.

teach.h: Key influencers: who people listen to
teach.body: Key influencers are the people who can shape the perception of the majority in the organizational ecosystem. Through their network, they have the greatest influence on the adoption of the change outcomes and the realization of benefits. They are found by asking who the affected group trusts, not by reading the organization chart. A respected sceptic can be a key influencer; so can an informal leader with no management title.

teach.h: Finding the key influencer in a people list

steps.label: Name the group
steps.sub: Whose adoption does the stem ask about?

steps.label: Look for trust
steps.sub: Respected by, belongs to or leads that group

steps.label: Check the network
steps.sub: Can shape how most of them see the change

steps.label: Drop look-alikes
steps.sub: Supplier, specialist, sponsor without that network

teach.caption: The same people list can give a different key influencer for a different group.
Seniority, expertise or a contract does not make someone a key influencer for a group they are not part of.

teach.body: Culture is the shared attitudes, values, goals and practices of a group: how things are really done. It decides whether a change is adopted, so read it from the scenario. Clues: leaders used to fixed plans, staff who have seen systems promised and dropped, fear of job losses, pride in professional judgement. Persistent non-compliance with new ways of working is a signal that they do not fit the culture: listen and adapt, rather than simply enforce.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3; PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1, 4.4

head: Clue in the scenario
OCM action that fits
rows: Frequent releases and demos build trust
Listen, address concerns, involve in design
Users in the team; co-create the product
Gather feedback and adapt the way of working
teach.caption: Agile ways of working support OCM: frequent releases, users in the team, testing, demos, retrospectives, feedback (4.2.4).

teach.body: Project manager Andrea Lucas lists stakeholders: engineers, operators, the union, the production manager, IT security, Senticore, customers needing 98% availability. Engineers doubt prediction, so she asks who they trust. The answer is Stuart Bell, not supplier director Dev Patel or data lead Hannah Reece. Stuart joins the shop-floor trial, helps present demos at progress reviews and feeds back concerns. Union representative Jim Halligan's question about monitoring workers is answered openly, early.

teach.caption: Relationships change over time, so revisit stakeholders and influencers as the project moves on (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.2).

teach.text: Classic trap: the key influencer is NOT the most senior person, the supplier who owns the contract, or the technical expert. It is the person whose network and credibility shape how the affected group sees the change. And a group that merely perceives itself affected is still a stakeholder.

items: Stakeholder: can affect, be affected by, or perceive itself affected by the change (4.2.2).
Key influencer: shapes the majority's perception through their network (4.2.2).
Start from the group in the stem; pick who that group trusts.
Sceptics and informal leaders can be key influencers; suppliers and specialists rarely are.
Read culture from clues; persistent non-compliance means listen and adapt.
Use agile working to help adoption: users in the team, demos, feedback, frequent releases.

summary: You can now identify every stakeholder in a scenario, including groups that only perceive themselves affected, and choose the key influencer for a named group from a people list. You can also read culture clues and pick the OCM action that fits them.

A.q: At Draycott, several maintenance engineers say a computer cannot tell them when a machine will fail. From the people list: Graham Doyle, operations director who holds the budget; Stuart Bell, senior engineer with 30 years' experience, respected by colleagues; Dev Patel, Senticore's account director; Hannah Reece, data science lead building the model. Who is MOST LIKELY to be a key influencer for the engineers?
options: Graham Doyle
Stuart Bell
Dev Patel
Hannah Reece
A.why: Key influencers shape the perception of the majority through their network (4.2.2). Stuart is respected by the engineers and is one of them, so his view will most influence their adoption.

whyNot.0: Graham is the senior sponsor, but seniority does not give him a trusted network among the engineers.
whyNot.2: Dev commits the supplier's fitting teams; he has no network among Draycott's engineers.
whyNot.3: Hannah is the technical expert behind the model, which is exactly what the engineers doubt.

A.q: At Saltmarsh Housing Group, contact centre advisers fear that online repair reporting will cost them their jobs. From the people list: Ellen Price, digital team lead; Frank Tolley, Coastline's operations manager; Amara Okeke, data and insight analyst; Kyle Morgan, experienced adviser and informal leader who trains new starters. Who is MOST LIKELY to be a key influencer for the advisers?
options: Ellen Price
Frank Tolley
Amara Okeke
Kyle Morgan
A.why: Kyle is an informal leader inside the adviser team and trains new starters, so his network gives him the most influence over how advisers see the change (4.2.2).

whyNot.0: Ellen configures the portal; she is not part of the advisers' network.
whyNot.1: Frank runs the contractor's engineers, a different group from the contact centre advisers.
whyNot.2: Amara measures performance; her expertise does not give her influence among advisers.

A.q: At Larkspur Rail, the union for train conductors says automatic delay compensation could change conductors' duties, although the project team believes conductors will not be affected. The project manager asks whether the union should appear in the stakeholder analysis. What is the BEST answer?
options: Yes, because it perceives itself to be affected by the change
No, because the change will not in fact affect the conductors
No, because it holds no role in the project management team
Yes, because a union represents users on the project board
A.why: A stakeholder includes anyone who perceives itself to be affected by the change initiative, not just those who are actually affected (4.2.2).

whyNot.1: Whether the effect is real does not matter: perceiving an effect is enough to be a stakeholder.
whyNot.2: Stakeholders are not limited to people with project roles.
whyNot.3: User representation on the board is a role matter; it is not why the union is a stakeholder.

B.q: At Callowmere University, many wellbeing staff are unsure about the Student Support Hub. From the people list: Daniel Ferreira, head of the web team; Ian Prothero, Northmere's account manager; Tom Brierley, experienced mental health adviser, respected by colleagues and openly doubtful about the hub; Sinead Walsh, independent quality manager. Who is MOST LIKELY to be a key influencer for the wellbeing staff?
options: Daniel Ferreira
Ian Prothero
Tom Brierley
Sinead Walsh
B.why: Tom is respected inside the wellbeing service, so through his network he can shape how colleagues see the hub (4.2.2). Being doubtful does not stop him being a key influencer; it makes engaging him more important.

whyNot.0: Daniel leads the web team, not the wellbeing staff whose adoption is in question.
whyNot.1: Ian represents the supplier; he has no network among wellbeing staff.
whyNot.3: Sinead is independent of the wellbeing service, so she lacks the network that shapes their view.

B.q: Callowmere wants students to trust and use the new hub from Welcome Week. From the people list: Rebecca Lyle, who manages the web team's backlog; Maya Kowalczyk, students' union vice-president for welfare and elected student representative; Chloe Hartley, Scrum master of the web team; Peter Langley, academic registrar. Who is MOST LIKELY to be a key influencer for students?
options: Rebecca Lyle
Maya Kowalczyk
Chloe Hartley
Peter Langley
B.why: This stem asks about STUDENTS. Maya is their elected representative with a network across the student body, so she can shape the majority's perception (4.2.2).

whyNot.0: Rebecca knows the backlog, but she has no network among students.
whyNot.2: Chloe facilitates the web team's events; she does not shape students' views.
whyNot.3: Peter is a senior administrator, but seniority is not the same as influence with students.

B.q: At Easterholm County Council, social workers keep recording assessments by phone and on paper instead of trying the online self-assessment in test sessions. Many have said they fear their professional judgement will be bypassed. Which action is MOST LIKELY to help adoption?
options: Raise the non-use as an issue for the programme board to decide
Send a council-wide message stressing the grant deadline
Add a target for online use to each social worker's appraisal
Listen to the concerns and adapt how their judgement is used
B.why: Persistent non-compliance signals that the new way of working does not fit the culture. Communication is as much about listening as broadcasting, addressing concerns before they become bigger risks (4.4), and co-creating with users helps adoption.

whyNot.0: Escalating to the board treats a culture signal as a decision for governance rather than listening to the people affected.
whyNot.1: A generic message is rarely effective and does not address the fear behind the behaviour (4.4).
whyNot.2: An appraisal target pushes compliance, which does not evolve the culture that makes change last.

C.q: At Pinewick Home and Garden, store managers are worried about extra work in the spring peak. The project manager plans to ask Elena Marsh, client services director at Tallis Logistics Software, who commits Tallis staff and owns the contract, to act as the key influencer for store managers. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because she commits supplier staff and owns the contract
Yes, because suppliers are stakeholders who can affect the change
No, because she lacks a network that shapes store managers' views
No, because a key influencer must be a member of the project board
C.why: A key influencer shapes the perception of the majority of the affected group through their network (4.2.2). Elena has no such network among Pinewick's store managers.

whyNot.0: Commercial authority over supplier staff gives no influence over store managers' perceptions.
whyNot.1: True that Tallis is a stakeholder, but that does not make Elena a key influencer for store managers.
whyNot.3: Key influencers are defined by network influence, not by a board seat.

C.q: At Draycott, the project manager invites Stuart Bell, a respected senior engineer who is sceptical about prediction, to join the shop-floor trial team and to help present each demo to other engineers. Is this an appropriate application of OCM, and why?
options: Yes, because his network lets him shape the engineers' view
Yes, because his long experience makes him the best tester
No, because sceptics should join after benefits are proven
No, because a key influencer should be the most senior person
C.why: Stuart is a key influencer: through his network he can shape how most engineers see the change (4.2.2). Involving him in co-creation and demos supports adoption (4.2.4).

whyNot.1: His experience may help testing, but that does not explain why involving him helps the organizational change.
whyNot.2: Engaging respected sceptics early lets concerns be heard and addressed before they become bigger risks.
whyNot.3: Seniority does not define a key influencer; network influence over the group does.

C.q: At Easterholm, the project manager builds the stakeholder list from the project management team structure: board members, the digital team, Abacus Care Software and the project office. The county carers' network is left off because it has no project role. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the communication approach covers everyone else
Yes, because people without project roles are reached via the board
No, because the carers' network must be given a seat on the board
No, because anyone affected or who feels affected is a stakeholder
C.why: Stakeholders include any individual, group or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by the change (4.2.2). Carers are directly affected by Care Online.

whyNot.0: The communication management approach is built from the stakeholder analysis, so leaving carers out of the list weakens it.
whyNot.1: Relying on the board to reach unlisted groups does not fix an incomplete stakeholder list.
whyNot.2: Stakeholders do not need board seats; the flaw is leaving them out of the analysis.

reteach.title: Who would the group text first?
reteach.question: If the engineers at Draycott had a group chat, whose message would change their minds fastest?

blocks.body: Picture each affected group as a group chat. The key influencer is the person whose message everyone reads and repeats. It might be a long-serving engineer, an informal leader who trains new starters, or an elected representative. The supplier, the data expert and the director are usually not in that chat at all.

children.edge: In or trusted by the group?
children.label: Yes: test their reach

blocks.text: Change the group, change the answer. The key influencer for students is not the key influencer for staff. Always reread which group the stem names.

explain.body: Any individual, group or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by the change. No project role is needed.

test.q: Saltmarsh's tenants' panel has no role in the project management team, but believes the new repairs service will change how tenants are treated. How should the project manager regard the panel?
options: As outside the project until it gains a role
As a stakeholder in the change initiative
As a supplier under the commercial approach
As project assurance for the tenants' view
test.why: It can be affected by and perceives itself to be affected by the change, so it is a stakeholder (4.2.2).

whyNot.0: A project role is not needed to be a stakeholder.
whyNot.2: The panel supplies no products or services under contract.
whyNot.3: Project assurance is a board-appointed role giving independent monitoring; the panel holds no such role.

explain.body: The person who can shape the perception of the majority of the affected group and, through their network, has the greatest influence on adoption and benefits. Find the group first, then the person it trusts.

test.q: Easterholm needs carers to try the new online carers' self-assessment. From the people list: Bev Lomax, chair of the county carers' network and a carer herself; Martin Sallis, Abacus account manager; Amy Fletcher, senior user researcher; Oliver Grant, delivery manager. Who is MOST LIKELY to be a key influencer for carers?
options: Bev Lomax
Martin Sallis
Amy Fletcher
Oliver Grant
test.why: Bev chairs a 600-member carers' network and is a carer herself, so her network shapes how carers see the change (4.2.2).

whyNot.1: Martin represents the supplier and has no network among carers.
whyNot.2: Amy has researched with carers, but research experience is not a trusted network among them.
whyNot.3: Oliver runs the digital team's events; he does not shape carers' views.

explain.body: Culture is the shared attitudes, values, goals and practices of a group. Read it from the scenario: past failures, fear for jobs, pride in judgement, preference for fixed plans. Persistent non-compliance means the new way does not yet fit: listen and adapt.
explain.cite: PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3; PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4

test.q: At Pinewick, store teams in the pilot keep logging collection orders on paper instead of the new handheld screen. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Ask area managers to enforce the screen at each store
Remove the paper forms from the pilot stores at once
Gather feedback from store teams on why it does not fit
Report the stores as non-compliant on the dashboard
test.why: Persistent non-compliance signals that the way of working does not fit how people actually work; gather and act on feedback, listening as much as broadcasting (4.4).

whyNot.0: Enforcement may secure compliance briefly, but it does not find or fix the mismatch.
whyNot.1: Removing the fallback without understanding the problem risks failed collections in the pilot.
whyNot.3: Making the stores visible as non-compliant does not address the cause.

explain.body: Users in the delivery team, frequent testing, demos in progress reviews, retrospectives, regular feedback and frequent releases all bring users closer to the product, so adoption is smoother and faster. Key influencers are ideal people to involve.

test.q: At Larkspur Rail, the passenger panel's chair is a daily commuter trusted by panel members. Which use of him is MOST LIKELY to support passengers' adoption of the Fair Fares app?
options: Ask him to approve the release map for each stage
Invite him to test increments and attend demos
Give him authority over the app team's backlog
Ask him to write the passenger section of the canvas
test.why: Frequent testing raises user engagement and demos in progress reviews speed adoption (4.2.4); involving a key influencer spreads that through his network.

whyNot.0: Approving the release map is a board decision, not a passenger role.
whyNot.2: The product backlog is owned by the product owner, not a passenger representative.
whyNot.3: The project canvas is led by the executive in starting up; this does not use his influence on adoption.
